📌 Liquidity Pools: How passive income can quietly burn your coins

Key Takeaways
⏺ Adding coins to a DEX liquidity pool earns you a share of trading fees
⏺ Impermanent Loss occurs when the price of one asset moves faster than the other
⏺ This post explains why just holding coins in your wallet is sometimes better than DeFi farming

1️⃣ Pool Mechanics — You always deposit two assets in a strict 50/50 value ratio, like ETH and USDT. The DEX smart contract continuously shifts this ratio based on what other traders buy or sell.
2️⃣ The Trap — If ETH pumps hard, arbitrageurs will drain the cheaper ETH out of your pool, leaving you with more stablecoins (USDT). As a result, you end up with fewer ETH tokens than you started with.
3️⃣ Why it is Impermanent — The loss remains on paper as long as your assets stay in the pool. If the price of ETH returns to the exact level it was when you deposited, the loss vanishes.
4️⃣ Real Loss — If you withdraw your funds while the price gap is wide, the loss becomes permanent. Frequently, this deficit is much larger than all the trading fees you collected.
5️⃣ Practice — To minimize risk, start with pools made of two stablecoins (like USDT/USDC) or highly correlated pairs (like WBTC/BTC). Impermanent loss there is practically non-existent.

Final Thoughts

Liquidity pool yield is your compensation for the risk of being left holding the weaker asset. Before rushing into farming, check if a simple buy-and-hold strategy serves you better.

On Sunday, as Washington and Tehran tried to choreograph the final steps of a framework deal, Israel sent its own message over Beirut in the form of bombs.

The Israeli military said it struck a Hezbollah command site on the southern outskirts of the Lebanese capital, in the Dahiya neighborhood, after the group launched drones and rockets toward northern Israel. 

Additional airstrikes were reported in the Tyre district and other parts of southern Lebanon, and Hezbollah confirmed the death of one of its operatives near Tyre.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz framed the attack in familiar terms, declaring that Israel “will not tolerate firing at its territory.” 

At the same time, the army acknowledged that it was preparing for possible retaliatory fire in the hours ahead, underscoring how quickly a single strike could widen the confrontation.

The timing is not incidental. Israel and the United States have been fighting a joint war against Iran since late February, and Hezbollah’s involvement has turned Lebanon into a parallel front. 

Iran has insisted that any agreement with Washington must cover the Lebanese arena as well, while Israel has tried to keep its campaign against Hezbollah formally separate from the Iran talks, in which it has no seat at the table.

From Tehran, Iran’s lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, condemned the strike in Dahiya and suggested that Washington was either unwilling or unable to restrain Israeli operations around Beirut. 

If the United States cannot deliver on its commitments, he implied, the “path” of negotiations cannot continue in its current form.

Hezbollah, for its part, has already rejected a U.S.-brokered cease-fire plan for Lebanon, with its leader portraying a truce between Israel and the Lebanese government as a form of capitulation for the movement. 

That leaves the situation in an uneasy limbo: formal diplomacy moving toward a fragile framework, while the actors on the ground test each other’s limits with incremental escalation.

Israel’s military command describes the moment as “sensitive and complex,” maintaining high alert and signaling readiness for both defensive and offensive scenarios. 

For now there were no immediate reports of casualties in Israel, and Lebanese authorities had yet to release full figures from the Dahiya strike. But the pattern is clear: each round of fire in Lebanon now doubles as a stress test for a still-unfinished deal between Washington and Tehran.
